title: OSPF Neighbors: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Two O S P F routers meet on a link. They don't automatically become neighbours. That only happens if a few details match.

scenes.heading: The neighbourhood watch
scenes.narration: Picture a gated community where every house waves a flag every ten seconds. The flag shows the house name, the street, and a secret handshake code. If a house stops waving for forty seconds, the others assume it's empty and cross it off. Those waves are hello packets, and forty seconds is the dead interval. For two houses to become neighbours, their street, handshake and timers must all match.

scenes.heading: What must match
scenes.narration: Here's the checklist. Area, subnet, timers, authentication and stub flags must all match. The process I D and the router I D do not need to match at all.

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three things catch people out. Process I Ds are local, and can differ. O S P F does not negotiate timers, so a mismatch means no neighbour. And the router I D does not need to be on the link's subnet.

items.right: No: they just won't form a neighbour

items.wrong: Router ID must be an interface on the link
